claims.statement: Consent to psychiatric treatment is described in professional guidance as a continuing process that is reviewed, revised, and renewed as circumstances change; a signed form or a documented consent discussion is evidence that the discussion took place at a moment in time and is not itself the consent.
claims.scope: A Canadian Psychiatric Association position paper stating Canadian common-law and provincial requirements for consent to psychiatric treatment. It describes a professional and legal position for one country, not an empirical finding and not a universal rule.
claims.uncertainty: Other jurisdictions reach comparable practical positions by different legal routes, state them differently, or leave them to professional regulation. The paper is a professional position and has not been re-verified against any later Canadian revision.

claims.statement: Giving consent does not oblige a person to accept what was proposed and does not remove their right to withdraw consent at any time, with narrow exceptions where stopping would itself be dangerous.
claims.scope: The same Canadian position paper, stating the position under Canadian law for treatment consent.
claims.uncertainty: The scope of the exceptions and the procedure for acting on a withdrawal are jurisdiction-specific and are not taught here.

claims.statement: Disclosure adequate for informed consent covers the nature and purpose of what is proposed, its likely benefits and probable risks, reasonable alternatives, the consequences of declining, and the identity of the person who will provide it; guidance also treats it as preferable that the person obtaining consent is the person delivering the treatment.
claims.scope: Canadian professional guidance, which frames the standard of disclosure around what a reasonable person in the patient's position would want to know.
claims.uncertainty: The legal standard of disclosure differs between jurisdictions, and some use a professional standard instead of a patient-centred one. The list is stated here as a checkable set of items and not as a legal test.

claims.statement: An agreement counts as voluntary only when it is free of conditions and influences that limit or control the choice; professional guidance names institutional restrictions, fear, coercion, undue influence, and misrepresentation among the circumstances that compromise it.
claims.scope: Canadian professional guidance on consent to psychiatric treatment.
claims.uncertainty: Whether any particular arrangement, such as asking about a student in a waiting area, crosses into undue influence is this lesson's own judgement about an invented case and is not a finding of the source.

claims.statement: Capacity to consent is assessed against a particular decision at a particular time and turns on the ability to understand the relevant information and to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding either way; having a psychiatric condition, disagreeing with the proposed treatment, or making a decision the clinician considers unwise does not by itself establish incapacity.
claims.scope: Canadian professional guidance drawing on Canadian case law. Stated here only as a boundary condition on the consent model; this lesson does not teach capacity assessment.
claims.uncertainty: Statutory tests for capacity and the procedures that follow a finding of incapacity differ substantially between jurisdictions.

claims.statement: The legal requirements for consent differ between jurisdictions within a single country: some Canadian provinces have enacted consent legislation codifying common-law principles while others have not, Quebec's civil law provides different procedures again, and clinicians are expected to know the requirements of the province or territory where they practise.
claims.scope: Canada, as described by a national professional association in 2015. Used in the lesson as a demonstration that variation exists inside one country, not as a description of Canadian law for any reader to rely on.
claims.uncertainty: The specific provincial statutes named in the source may have been amended since 2015, and no comparison across countries is claimed.

claims.statement: Confidentiality has limits fixed by the law of a particular place, and those limits differ sharply between jurisdictions: in the United States, statutory duties to warn or protect a third party after Tarasoff are mandatory in roughly 27 to 33 states, permissive in roughly 9 to 11, and absent from statute in roughly 6 to 13, the ranges reflecting disagreement about how particular statutes should be classified, and clinicians are expected to know the law of the state where they practise.
claims.scope: United States law as summarised in a 2020 emergency-medicine review. The counts describe state statutes as classified by that review and say nothing about any other country.
claims.uncertainty: The counts are ranges because classification is itself disputed, statutes change, and the review is not a legal authority. Countries outside the United States handle the question through professional regulation, general law, or other statutory schemes not covered here.

claims.statement: Among respondents to two national United States surveys who reported experiencing depression, suicidal thoughts, abuse, or sexual assault, 47.5% in one sample and 40.0% in the other said they had withheld at least one of those from a clinician; the reasons endorsed most often included embarrassment, not wanting to be judged or lectured, not wanting to undertake difficult follow-up, and not wanting the information in their medical record, the last named by 57.1% and 52.7%.
claims.scope: Two United States online survey samples recruited through a crowdworking platform and a survey panel in 2015, describing self-reported behaviour across a respondent's lifetime of clinical contacts.
claims.uncertainty: Self-report about past encounters is subject to recall and selection effects, the samples are not representative of any clinical population, and nothing in the study observes what happened in any consultation. The figures show what people say they were avoiding and do not establish how often withholding occurs in practice.

claims.statement: In a two-year study of 170 adolescents discharged from psychiatric hospital and asked repeatedly about suicidal ideation, more frequent assessment was not followed by higher later ideation scores, and more than half the group scored lower at the end than at the start; the authors report the study as uncontrolled and unable to establish a mechanism.
claims.scope: One study of 170 adolescents already receiving psychiatric treatment in the United States, using a single self-report ideation questionnaire over two years.
claims.uncertainty: There was no control group, so regression to the mean and the effect of ongoing treatment cannot be separated from the effect of assessment. The result concerns ideation scores only and does not address attempts or deaths. It is used in this lesson only to counter the specific belief that asking creates the thought, and it supports no recommendation about asking any real person.

claims.statement: In a survey at one Portuguese university hospital covering 185 psychiatry patients and 185 paediatric participants, 75% of the psychiatry respondents who recalled the encounter said the physician had asked whether they minded medical students being present, while 31% said the students had introduced themselves as medical students and asked permission; some psychiatry respondents reported that a student's presence made disclosing an intimate problem harder.
claims.scope: One teaching hospital in Porto, Portugal, reported in 2023; patient self-report of what they recalled, with respondents who did not remember excluded from both percentages.
claims.uncertainty: A single-centre survey in one health system, dependent on recall, cannot be generalised to other services or countries, and the two percentages have slightly different denominators because of the exclusions.

claims.statement: Whether the general consent a patient signs on admission covers a student observing a clinical encounter, or whether explicit consent should be sought for each observation, is a contested convention; a United States emergency-medicine review records both positions and states separately that visitors should be present only with the patient's permission.
claims.scope: A 2006 United States emergency-medicine review, cited to establish that the disagreement exists rather than to state what any policy requires.
claims.uncertainty: The source is nearly two decades old and institutional policy, professional guidance, and law have moved in many places since. Any learner needs the current policy of their own institution and jurisdiction, which this claim does not supply.

claims.statement: A systematic review of 28 studies found professional interpreters associated with fewer communication errors and with better comprehension, service use, clinical outcomes, and satisfaction than ad hoc interpreters such as family members, accompanying friends, and untrained bilingual staff.
claims.scope: A 2007 systematic review of literature published to September 2005, predominantly United States studies of patients with limited English proficiency in general medical settings.
claims.uncertainty: Most included studies were observational, so the review reports associations. The review notes that a quarter of included studies did not separate professional from ad hoc interpreters and half did not state whether the professional interpreters were trained. No included study is a psychiatric assessment, and the evidence base predates current remote-interpreting arrangements.

claims.statement: A systematic review of 179 studies from 111 publications, covering 28,570,712 consultations in 67 countries, found average primary-care consultation length ranging from 48 seconds in Bangladesh to 22.5 minutes in Sweden, with 18 countries representing about 50% of the global population at five minutes or less.
claims.scope: Primary-care consultations, from literature searched to 2016. The figures are national averages and none of the included data describes a psychiatric assessment.
claims.uncertainty: The review reports that its analyses rest on average consultation lengths and do not separate rural from urban or public from private practice, that measurement methods differed between studies, and that about a quarter of included studies were rated poor quality. The figures are used here only to show the size of the variation between health systems.

claims.statement: After patients at three German psychiatric outpatient clinics gained online access to their clinical notes, a comparison of 876 notes from 97 patients before and after found significant changes in eleven linguistic features: stigmatising, controlling, demeaning, and incomprehensible language decreased while comprehensible, personal, resource-oriented, and positive emotional language increased; the clinicians interviewed said the substantive content of their documentation was unchanged and described handling sensitive material through more general phrasing.
claims.scope: Three psychiatric outpatient clinics in Germany, comparing documentation before and after the introduction of patient online access, with interviews of ten healthcare professionals.
claims.uncertainty: There is no control site, so the study cannot establish that patient access caused the changes it measured. Clinicians' own accounts of leaving content unchanged are self-report. The result describes one health system and one implementation.
